A rare triple-star system has been found just 28 light-years away. Led by Étienne Artigau of the University of Montreal’s Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets, the team identified a red dwarf with two white dwarf companions.

Gemini North in Hawaii captured the closer white dwarf directly for the first time. It was once a star about 40% more massive than the Sun, expanding into a giant hundreds of times its original size. The nearby red dwarf survived and now shares a wide, stable orbit with it. “This system should not exist,” said co-author Patrick Dufour.

Named Welopōʻai, the system is the only known example of its kind within 100 light-years. Studying it could shed light on how stars evolve and die.

Astronomy & Astrophysics (2026). DOI: 10.1051/0004-6361/202661214
